# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **Its caption:** a title and a sentence or two, written from the fact sheet.

A caption says nothing the fact sheet does not say. What a project taught the person, what was wrong before they came, how often a thing is used: those are theirs to tell you. Where you want such a sentence and do not have it, write the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

Question: **What's worth fixing, and how do you know it's fixed?** Object: five snag tags — small numbered tabs on string, the kind tied to a fault on site. One tag per thing she does: Calder Court, Kirk Street, A School That Grows, the Cabin at Kashuby, and her teaching at Clyde School. At rest they hang, loose, off the plain outline of an ordinary building. --- ## The chapters | Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1. Location | Location | Where from | The places and years; what she learned from | All five tags scatter onto a map/timeline and settle | Hover or tap a tag for its dates; tap the workshop/book markers for the one line each | | 4. Item | Item | How she works | The documents she works from, in her words | Tags regroup into a row and turn to show what each found wrong | Tap a tag to read its line; scroll also reveals each in turn | | 5. To the side, on its own: Teaching, labelled "ongoing" | Nothing else | Closed: Kirk Street occupied; the cabin built and lived in. Open: the school shortlisted, not built; Calder Court modelled, not measured — monitoring starts this winter. Teaching doesn't close — it runs every week. | ### 7. Close | Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 7.1 | 1 | All five tags settle into one quiet row at the foot of the page. Everything is still, except the Calder Court tag, which keeps its faint swing | Final tag faces, unchanged from Status | Nothing else | In two years, Marta wants her own practice. Until then: an old house, a small plot, or a school that needs a guest critic are all reasons to write. [contact method — see below] | --- ## Someone with thirty seconds The first screen (1.1) carries her name, her title, one line of what she does, the question, and one proof figure (96 flats; 68%, modelled). The rail, visible from the first screen on, jumps to any chapter by name. One link from the first screen skips straight to the close, for contact. --- ## Without the scene | Where | What the visitor gets | |---|---| | On a phone | The same seven chapters, one column, same real photos and captions. The scatter, the unfolding and the sort become shorter, simpler motions — the tags still move, but in fewer steps, and the exhibits in chapter 5 play as a straightforward sequence rather than a scene the visitor can orbit. The rail becomes a bottom sheet or a small menu. | | With reduced motion | Every beat still exists, but the pieces jump straight to each beat's settled state — no scatter, no unfolding, no swing. The Calder Court tag's open status is said in words ("not yet measured") rather than shown by motion. | | With no WebGL | Flat illustrations stand in for the 3D scene: a drawn version of each tag, in the same positions the beats describe, as ordinary images. All text, captions and real photographs are unchanged. | | With no JavaScript | A single plain HTML page, the seven chapters in order, headed by their names, with every real photograph, drawing and caption present as ordinary text and images — no tags, no motion, nothing missing in substance. | --- ## The look and the type Three looks, each named by the object's own material. Pick by scrolling, once it's built. **A. Site.** Ground: concrete grey. Ink: near-black. Accent: the orange of snag-tag string. Pieces: matte kraft card, slightly worn, numbers stamped as if stencilled on site. **B. Drawing.** Ground: cream, like tracing paper. Ink: graphite. Accent: a single snag-red. Pieces: thin card with fine linework on their faces, as if drawn rather than printed. **C. Timber.** Ground: pale ply. Ink: charcoal. Accent: the orange of builder's twine. Pieces: thin plywood, numbers burned in rather than printed — closest to the cabin's own material. Two typefaces: a plain humanist sans for all reading text, and a stencilled, site-stamp face for whatever's printed on the tags themselves — the only place the form's own voice appears in the type. --- ## Everything else the site needs | | Build, later or never | Who decided | |---|---|---| | The way round the page (the rail) | Build | Me — a one-page scroll needs a way to jump and to skip, or the thirty-second read fails | | A page for each project | Later | Me, to confirm with Marta — five tags carry enough for one page now; a deeper page per project is more than this version needs | | Every project listed | Build | Already settled — all five appear | | How to reach her, and a CV | Build the contact action; **CV open** | Marta, still to say: no email or form was given, and her cv.md carries an out-of-date title ("Senior Architect") she's already corrected to Associate — needs a decision on whether a downloadable CV exists at all, and if so, which contact address | | What others say | Never, for now | Already decided (`decided-for-you.md`) — no testimonial exists; none will be invented | | Languages | Build: English only | Me, by default — all material is in English; flag if Polish matters to her, given Gdansk | | What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | Build | Me — the preview image should come from the cabin material, since it's hers outright and needs no permission; favicon likely a single snag tag | | The page for an address that is not there | Build | Me — small, in the form's own voice | | A blog | Never, unless asked | Me, by default — nothing in the material calls for one | | A chat | Never | Me, by default — not fitting for a site aimed at direct enquiries | | A legal notice | Later | Me, to confirm with Marta — revisit once she's taking enquiries directly rather than through the practice, and once it's decided what a contact form collects | --- ## What I'm asking for A yes to this script, or what to change in it. Two things still need her word before anything is built, beyond the yes: the practice's and Tom Reid's permission for Calder Court's and Kirk Street's photographs and drawings (chapter 5, beats 5.1–5.2), and a contact address or form for the close. Everything else here either stands on a confirmed fact or is marked, in the table above, as mine to decide and hers to overrule.

Here's the full script, written to the snag-list concept. It's also in `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

**The idea.** A snag list is the document an architect carries at the end of a job — one item per fault, open until it's closed out. The site repoints it to open the story instead: every building Marta's touched is an item, open until closed. The object is five snag tags on string — Calder Court, Kirk Street, A School That Grows, the Cabin at Kashuby, and her teaching — hanging off the plain outline of an ordinary building at rest.

**The question the page answers:** *What's worth fixing, and how do you know it's fixed?*

## The seven chapters, in order

**1. Opening.** One tag hangs off a bare building outline. On screen, unscrolled: her name, title, the question, and one proof figure (96 flats; 68% less heating demand, modelled). This is the whole thirty-second read — a rail to jump to any chapter, and a link straight to contact, are both visible from here.

**2. Logged by.** The same tag turns to show its back: her standing to say any of this — Associate, ARB since 2023. Caption is her own words, from her profile: *"the most useful thing an architect can do is make an old building worth keeping."*

**3. Location.** All five tags lift off and scatter onto a map: Gdansk twice, Glasgow three times, with her degrees and jobs landing as each tag settles. Two small, non-tag markers sit alongside — a workbench and a book — tappable for what she learned from: her father's workshop, and a book of Swiss timber joints she's had since nineteen.

**4. Item.** The tags regroup and turn face-forward, each showing what it found wrong: a cold 1960s block, an empty hall, a bare plot, a brief for a school that needs room to grow. The teaching tag shows something different — a studio, Tuesdays — since teaching isn't a fault to fix. Caption names what she actually works from: the drawing set in order, the RIBA stages nought to seven, the snag list itself.

**5. Action taken — the main weight of the page.** Each tag unfolds in turn into its own exhibit:
- *Calder Court:* the tag becomes a layered wall section, building up insulation, membrane, cladding. She's named as project architect from technical design to handover — concept was a partner's. The 68% figure is stated as modelled, not measured, monitoring starting this winter.
- *Kirk Street:* unfolds into the section through the hall, becoming six flats.
- *The cabin:* unfolds into the timber frame itself, raised piece by piece from her own 200 photographs and time-lapse — the one piece needing nobody's permission but hers.
- *The school:* unfolds to show only the structure and sections she drew, labelled "with a team of four."
- *Teaching:* stays flat — a line of text, no exhibit.

**6. Status.** The tags fold flat and sort into Closed (Kirk Street, the cabin) and Open (the school, Calder Court). Calder Court's tag doesn't join either pile — it hangs apart with a faint, slow swing, because its figure genuinely hasn't been checked yet.

**7. Close.** All five tags settle into a quiet row. Everything stops moving except Calder Court's tag. Caption: what she wants next — her own practice in two years; until then, an old house, a small plot, or a school needing a guest critic — and how to reach her.

## What a visitor can click

A rail (visible from the first screen) jumps to any chapter by name. In chapter 5, clicking a project's tag jumps straight to its exhibit. Tags are hoverable/tappable throughout for their one-line facts (dates in chapter 3, status in chapter 6). One link from the first screen skips straight to contact.

## The look and type

Three options, named by the object's own material — pick once it's built, by scrolling through each:

- **Site:** concrete grey ground, near-black ink, snag-string orange accent, matte worn kraft tags.
- **Drawing:** cream tracing-paper ground, graphite ink, a single snag-red accent, fine linework on the tags' faces.
- **Timber:** pale ply ground, charcoal ink, builder's-twine orange accent, numbers burned into thin plywood — closest to the cabin's own material.

Two typefaces throughout: a plain humanist sans for all reading text, and a stencilled site-stamp face only for what's printed on the tags.

## On a phone, and without the 3D

| Where | What you get |
|---|---|
| Phone | Same seven chapters, one column, same real photos and captions. Scatter/unfold/sort become shorter and simpler, chapter 5's exhibits play as a plain sequence rather than something you orbit. Rail becomes a bottom sheet. |
| Reduced motion | Pieces jump straight to each beat's settled state. Calder Court's open status is said in words, not shown by swinging. |
| No WebGL | Flat drawn illustrations stand in for every 3D moment, same positions, same text and photos. |
| No JavaScript | One plain HTML page, all seven chapters, every real photo and caption present as ordinary text and images. Nothing in substance is missing. |

## Everything else the site needs

| Item | Build / later / never | Decided by |
|---|---|---|
| The rail (way round the page) | Build | Me |
| A page per project | Later | Me, to confirm with you |
| Every project listed | Build | Settled |
| Contact method, and a CV | Build contact; **CV still open** | You — no email/form given yet, and the cv.md title is out of date |
| Testimonials | Never, for now | Already decided — none exist, none invented |
| Languages | English only | Me, by default |
| Shared-link preview and site icon | Build, from the cabin material | Me |
| 404 page | Build, in the form's own voice | Me |
| Blog | Never, unless asked | Me, by default |
| Chat | Never | Me, by default |
| Legal notice | Later | Me, to confirm once you're taking enquiries directly |

**Two things still need your word before anything is built,** beyond a yes to this: permission from the practice and from Tom Reid for the Calder Court/Kirk Street photos and drawings, and a contact address or form for the close.

Is this a yes, or is there something to change?

**2. Logged by.** The same tag turns to show its back: her standing to say any of this — Associate, ARB since 2023. Caption is her own words, from her profile: *"the most useful thing an architect can do is make an old building worth keeping."*

**3. Location.** All five tags lift off and scatter onto a map: Gdansk twice, Glasgow three times, with her degrees and jobs landing as each tag settles. Two small, non-tag markers sit alongside — a workbench and a book — tappable for what she learned from: her father's workshop, and a book of Swiss timber joints she's had since nineteen.

**4. Item.** The tags regroup and turn face-forward, each showing what it found wrong: a cold 1960s block, an empty hall, a bare plot, a brief for a school that needs room to grow. The teaching tag shows something different — a studio, Tuesdays — since teaching isn't a fault to fix. Caption names what she actually works from: the drawing set in order, the RIBA stages nought to seven, the snag list itself.

**5. Action taken — the main weight of the page.** Each tag unfolds in turn into its own exhibit:
- *Calder Court:* the tag becomes a layered wall section, building up insulation, membrane, cladding. She's named as project architect from technical design to handover — concept was a partner's. The 68% figure is stated as modelled, not measured, monitoring starting this winter.
- *Kirk Street:* unfolds into the section through the hall, becoming six flats.
- *The cabin:* unfolds into the timber frame itself, raised piece by piece from her own 200 photographs and time-lapse — the one piece needing nobody's permission but hers.
- *The school:* unfolds to show only the structure and sections she drew, labelled "with a team of four."
- *Teaching:* stays flat — a line of text, no exhibit.

**6. Status.** The tags fold flat and sort into Closed (Kirk Street, the cabin) and Open (the school, Calder Court). Calder Court's tag doesn't join either pile — it hangs apart with a faint, slow swing, because its figure genuinely hasn't been checked yet.

**7. Close.** All five tags settle into a quiet row. Everything stops moving except Calder Court's tag. Caption: what she wants next — her own practice in two years; until then, an old house, a small plot, or a school needing a guest critic — and how to reach her.

## What a visitor can click

A rail (visible from the first screen) jumps to any chapter by name. In chapter 5, clicking a project's tag jumps straight to its exhibit. Tags are hoverable/tappable throughout for their one-line facts (dates in chapter 3, status in chapter 6). One link from the first screen skips straight to contact.

## The look and type

Three options, named by the object's own material — pick once it's built, by scrolling through each:

- **Site:** concrete grey ground, near-black ink, snag-string orange accent, matte worn kraft tags.
- **Drawing:** cream tracing-paper ground, graphite ink, a single snag-red accent, fine linework on the tags' faces.
- **Timber:** pale ply ground, charcoal ink, builder's-twine orange accent, numbers burned into thin plywood — closest to the cabin's own material.

Two typefaces throughout: a plain humanist sans for all reading text, and a stencilled site-stamp face only for what's printed on the tags.

## On a phone, and without the 3D

| Where | What you get |
|---|---|
| Phone | Same seven chapters, one column, same real photos and captions. Scatter/unfold/sort become shorter and simpler, chapter 5's exhibits play as a plain sequence rather than something you orbit. Rail becomes a bottom sheet. |
| Reduced motion | Pieces jump straight to each beat's settled state. Calder Court's open status is said in words, not shown by swinging. |
| No WebGL | Flat drawn illustrations stand in for every 3D moment, same positions, same text and photos. |
| No JavaScript | One plain HTML page, all seven chapters, every real photo and caption present as ordinary text and images. Nothing in substance is missing. |
